options.rationale: Correct: microorganisms need moisture.

options.content: It adds a layer of salt to the food that kills all the insects in it

stem: Which method is a **contemporary** way of preserving food?

options.content: smoking over the hearth
options.rationale: This is an indigenous method.

options.content: canning
options.rationale: Correct: food is heated and sealed in tins.

options.content: storing in a granary
options.rationale: This is an indigenous storage method.

options.content: mixing grain with ash
options.rationale: This is an indigenous way of keeping pests away.

explanation: Contemporary methods include canning, refrigeration, freezing, packaging and pasteurisation.

stem: Why is a traditional granary often **raised** on stones or poles?

options.content: so that the grain can be cooked inside it
options.rationale: Grain is not cooked in the granary.

options.content: to keep the grain dry and away from rats and termites
options.rationale: Correct: raising it protects against damp and pests.

options.content: to make the grain ripen faster after harvest
options.rationale: Grain is harvested when ripe; storage does not ripen it.

options.content: so that cattle can shelter underneath
options.rationale: This is not its purpose.

explanation: Raising the granary keeps damp from the ground and pests such as rats and termites away from the grain.

stem: Farai finds that groundnuts stored in a damp corner have grown mould. What should the family do?

options.content: Wash them and use them to make dovi
options.rationale: Washing does not remove poisons made by moulds.

options.content: Mix them with fresh groundnuts so the mould is diluted
options.rationale: This spreads the problem.

options.content: Feed them to small children because they are soft
options.rationale: This is dangerous.

options.content: Throw them away, because some moulds produce poisons
options.rationale: Correct: mouldy nuts can contain aflatoxins.

explanation: Mouldy groundnuts and grain can contain aflatoxins, which cause serious illness; they should be thrown away and stores kept dry.

stem: Why are **small grains** such as sorghum and millet important for food security in dry regions?

options.content: They grow only in very wet places
options.rationale: They are suited to dry areas.

options.content: They cannot be stored at all
options.rationale: Small grains store well.

options.content: They tolerate drought better than maize
options.rationale: Correct: they still yield in poor rainfall seasons.

options.content: They are imported every year
options.rationale: They are grown locally.

explanation: Small grains survive drought better than maize and store well, so they protect families in poor seasons.

stem: Which is the **strongest** reason for a rural family to keep using indigenous storage methods alongside shop-bought food?

options.content: They never allow any pests, damp or mould to reach the stored food at any time
options.rationale: Indigenous methods can also fail if not done well.

options.content: They make all food last for ever
options.rationale: No method makes food last for ever.

options.content: They are required by law in rural areas
options.rationale: There is no such law.

options.content: They are cheap and protect the family when prices rise or roads are cut
options.rationale: Correct: they support household food security.

explanation: Indigenous methods use little money and local materials, so a family's own stored food protects it from shortages and high prices.
hints: Think about cost and independence from shops.

stem: Mufushwa (umfushwa) is made by drying leafy vegetables.
explanation: True. Leaves such as pumpkin or cowpea leaves are blanched and sun-dried.

stem: Food that has thawed should be frozen again to keep it safe.
explanation: False. Thawed food should not be refrozen; it should be cooked and eaten, because bacteria may have multiplied while it thawed.

stem: Match each indigenous food (Shona / Ndebele) with what it is.

A second different method

stem: Explain **two** reasons why indigenous foods are important.

points.description: Identifies: nutrition
Develops: e.g. mopane worms and groundnuts provide protein; leafy vegetables provide vitamins and minerals
Identifies: food security / heritage / income / low cost
Develops: e.g. small grains tolerate drought and dried foods last through the dry season

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Indigenous foods are nutritious: mopane worms and groundnuts are rich in protein, and leafy vegetables provide vitamins and minerals. They also support food security, because small grains survive drought better than maize and dried foods last through the dry season.

explanation: One mark for each reason and one for its development.

stem: A school in Masvingo wants learners to value indigenous foods. Suggest **two** activities and explain how each would help.

points.description: Suggests a food fair / cooking day where families prepare indigenous dishes
Explains that learners taste the foods and learn recipes and preservation methods from elders
Suggests a school garden of small grains and indigenous vegetables / drying project
Explains that learners practise growing and preserving foods and see their value for food security

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: The school could hold an indigenous food fair where parents and grandparents cook dishes such as mufushwa with dovi, so learners taste them and learn recipes and methods from elders. It could also start a garden of small grains and indigenous vegetables and dry the harvest, so learners practise the methods and see how these foods protect families in dry years.

explanation: One mark for each activity and one for explaining its effect.
hints: Think about tasting, learning from elders and growing.

stem:
**Source A** — a description of a homestead in Gwanda written by a fictional student, 2026 (invented for this question)

> Behind the kitchen hut stands a small granary raised on flat stones, with a thatched lid. Inside the kitchen, strips of meat hang above the fire, and a clay pot sealed with mud holds sorghum seed for next season. My grandmother mixes a little ash into the beans before she stores them.

Read Source A and answer the questions.

stem: This question is about methods of storing and preserving food.

parts.label: (a)
parts.stem: Describe how **two** contemporary methods preserve food.

points.description: Names a contemporary method (e.g. refrigeration / freezing)
Describes how it works (cold slows or stops bacteria)
Names a second method (e.g. canning / packaging / pasteurisation)
Describes how it works (heat kills microorganisms and the sealed tin keeps air out)

answerSpec.markingNotes: Example answer: Freezing keeps food at very low temperatures so that bacteria cannot multiply. Canning heats food in sealed tins, killing microorganisms, and the seal keeps air and new germs out.

parts.label: (b)
parts.stem: "Indigenous methods of preserving food are better than contemporary methods." How far do you agree?

points.description: For indigenous: cheap, local materials, no electricity; support food security and heritage
For contemporary: longer storage, convenience, hygiene standards, variety, large-scale transport
Limitations: indigenous methods can fail with damp and pests; contemporary methods cost money and need electricity / power cuts
Supported judgement

levels.descriptor: Developed explanation of several relevant points or arguments, supported by accurate, specific knowledge and examples, considering more than one side and reaching a supported judgement that answers the question.
Developed explanation of some factors or arguments with relevant supporting detail; a judgement is attempted but is only partly supported, or the other side is thin.
Some explanation of one or two relevant factors, or several points described with limited explanation; little or no judgement.
Simple, general or narrative statements with limited relevance to the question; little explanation.

answerSpec.modelAnswer:
Indigenous methods have clear strengths. Sun-drying, smoking and granaries use local materials and no electricity, so they suit rural families and cost little. They keep food through the dry season and preserve heritage and knowledge.

Contemporary methods also have strengths. Freezing, canning and packaging keep food safe for longer, meet hygiene standards and allow food to be transported across the country, giving variety all year. However, they cost money and many depend on electricity, so power cuts can spoil frozen food. Indigenous methods can fail too, if grain is stored damp or pests get in.

I partly agree. Indigenous methods are better for cheap, independent household food security, while contemporary methods are better for convenience and large-scale supply. The best approach uses both, with good hygiene.

explanation: A practice evaluative item comparing indigenous and contemporary preservation.
hints: In (b), think about cost, electricity, hygiene and scale.
